newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Poor Russians cut back on coffee.
newsitem.headline: Poor Russians cut back on coffee.

text.p: Russians, who usually drink more coffee in the winter holiday season, are not buying as much as usual this year as a nationwide cash crisis takes erodes their incomes, traders said on Thursday.
Coffee importers say the Russian market has vast potential, with average per-capita consumption at a weak of 130 grams per year compared with neighbouring Finland's 1.5 kilograms.
But Russian demand over October-December, usually perkier than in other months, has flattened, a sign that consumer spending and the Russian economy are struggling to pick up.
"Russian demand is much more modest than it used to be in these months," said Antonio Ribeiro-Prestes of Brazil's Real Cafe-Moscow.
Traders blamed Russia's salary arrears crisis for cutting into consumer buying power and said importers lacked the cash needed to increase buying.
"The economic situation is quite tough; many people haven't been paid for months. Banks have cut trade financing since it is more profitable to buy Treasury bills," Ribeiro-Prestes said.
Coffee imports are battling for shelf space with tea, a more traditional drink in Russia.
Nevertheless, traders put total Russian coffee imports for 1996, including soluble brands, green beans and milled and roasted types, at 50,000 tonnes, above 1995's 40,000 tonnes.
But they warned that the figures could be misleading.
"This does not necessarily mean there has been a rise in imports. It's just that we know more about other firms' activities now," said one trader who declined to be named.
Official import statistics, based on customs declarations, often do not tell the whole story, since some coffee imports are brought in unregistered by traders avoiding import tariffs.
Sergei Feonov of former Soviet coffee monopoly importer Soyuzplodoimport said he thought wholesale demand had risen in September and October but that sales would slip before January.
"January always brings worries to the market; people expect all kinds of legislative changes," he said. "Our buyers want to be on the safe side and are ordering less for January-February."
Some of Russia's most prominent consumer goods importers are social funds and organisations that enjoy tax privileges and make big profits by importing coffee, tobacco and alcohol.

"One has the impression that the Russian Orthodox Church, the Russian Red Cross and Afghan war veterans drink more coffee than all the rest of Russia," said one trader, referring to groups importing large quantities of consumer goods.
Traders forecast a slight growth in Russian consumption in coming years and said new tariffs in 1997 were unlikely.
"It's unlikely they will introduce more duties, since last year the government ripped us off so much," Feonov said.

He also said there was a gentle rise in the amount of natural coffee sold in Russia, which he put at 15,000-20,000 tonnes a year. But Ribeiro-Prestes said natural coffee imports were flat at about 5,000 tonnes a year. The rest of the market was of instant brands, 30 percent of them of Brazilian origin.
Brazilian traders said they were worried by competition from European firms, such as Nestle SA of Switzerland, which are racing to create local distributing networks.
"We hope reliable importers will be interested in creating similar networks jointly with Brazilian producers to compete with European ones," Prestes said.
"Setting up distribution infrastructure is likely to be the main direction of the market over the next year."
